tagline: The Great Skyroad crosses alpine country on a seasonal mountain passage
intro: Wyoming Highway 130 crosses the Snowy Range on two lanes, rising from an 8,000-foot valley floor to 10,847 feet. Grades stay at or below 6.5 percent, and the drive takes approximately one hour without extended stops. The Forest Service highlights the alpine habitats, lakes and native wildflowers of this National Forest Scenic Byway. Sagebrush and lodgepole pine give way to spruce-fir forest and alpine country. Near the summit, wind shapes the trees known as krummholz in an old-growth spruce-fir forest. Turnouts and picnic areas provide places to pause along the crossing. Wildflowers grow in the alpine meadows throughout summer.

The Snowy Range Road began as a wagon trail in the 1870s. Highway construction started in the 1920s and took six years; the finished road became known as the Great Skyroad. Widening and improvements followed in the 1980s, and the road received National Forest Scenic Byway designation.

Driving from west to east, begin at the forest boundary in the Brush Creek valley. The western slope carries spruce, fir, aspen and pine forest below Silver Lake. Lake Marie and Mirror Lake lie below the summit, where Libby Flats offers a view south to Colorado. The eastern end of the byway is just outside Centennial.

moments.title: Lake Marie
moments.text: Medicine Bow Peak rises above Lake Marie and nearby Mirror Lake, below the summit of the byway. The peak belongs to a quartzite ridge with year-round snowfields on its flanks and glacial lakes at its base. Across from the Lake Marie parking area, a trailhead connects hiking routes on the south side of the road. At Mirror Lake, a shoreline path and fishing platform bring visitors to the water beneath the peaks. The picnic ground also includes a path to a historic CCC toilet building; its shoreline path, fishing platform and path to the water are accessible to people with disabilities.
moments.notice: Look for Medicine Bow Peak reflected in Lake Marie and Mirror Lake.

moments.title: Libby Flats
moments.text: At Libby Flats, the summit view reaches south to the Rawah and Never Summer wilderness areas in Colorado. The observation point also connects to a smaller story below the overlook: a short loop trail leads to Red Mask Mine and a nearby miner’s cabin. The mine operated in the 1920s. Interpretive signs explain the mine and cabin, then identify the sparse trees and low-growing flowers of this high-altitude setting. Strong winds and precipitation falling mostly as snow are part of that setting. Alongside the Libby Flats observation point at the summit is the Medicine Bow Peak overlook, another place to look across the high country.

moments.title: Centennial
moments.text: Centennial outlasted its first gold rush. Gold discovered on Centennial Ridge in 1875 drew miners to an old logging-camp site, where a community was reestablished in 1876. The name marked the United States’ hundredth anniversary. Most gold was gone by 1877, but merchants stayed to serve ranchers. The railway reached town in 1907; its depot, later moved a short distance, now houses the Nici Self Museum. The depot’s long frame building has broad overhanging eaves and a projecting bay designed to look down the tracks at its original location.

practical: Libby Flats: Snow closes the high road in winter. The Forest Service gives the normal driving season as Memorial Day through October. (checked 2026-10-11)
